View transitions drawn by a canvas

Five experiments in which startViewTransition() supplies the timing and a canvas draws the pictures. The content is HTML inside <canvas layoutsubtree>. Press the button under each one. The clocks show which pictures are live.

1. A WebGL shader timed by a transition scoped to the canvas

"Shuffle" calls canvas.startViewTransition() and reorders six HTML tiles. The browser animates a hidden group for each tile. The canvas reads each group's progress, turns the tile once about its vertical axis and lifts it toward the viewer. The fragment shader ripples the tile and splits its colour channels along the direction of travel.

2. A canvas-scoped transition inside a transition on its ancestor

The sidebar and the canvas are in a grid. One transition is scoped to the grid and resizes the sidebar. The other is scoped to the canvas and shuffles its tiles. Start them in either order. The checkbox removes view-transition-scope: all from the canvas, which changes the result of the first button.

3. view-transition-class with one canvas for each list item

Each row is its own canvas with one HTML child, a view-transition-name and the class row. The transition is scoped to the list and the browser moves the canvases. While it runs, each canvas draws its row in horizontal strips that bow sideways like a plucked string, further for rows that travel further.

4. The group box of a canvas child as the position to draw at

This one is a document transition. The white card is a child of the canvas with a view-transition-name. Its group has no picture, but it has the right box at every frame. The canvas reads that box and draws the card there, stretched along its direction of travel, with copies behind it. The orange label below is ordinary HTML in the same transition, moved by the browser.

Show the code read ::view-transition-group(), draw there
  1. The markup.
  2. The names. The canvas has a name so that its live picture is shown without a cross-fade.
  3. Read the group's box.
  4. Draw at the box, then put the hit box back. Without the last line the transition doesn't move: the browser takes the place of the last draw as the card's new position and retargets the group to it.

5. One canvas draws every change of a small app

The whole app below is one HTML element in one canvas. Every change (a tab, opening a message, the theme) goes through one function. It takes an ElementImage of the app as it is, starts a transition scoped to the canvas, changes the DOM, and draws from the old picture to the live app with the chosen effect.

The message body is ordinary HTML text. Select it, or go back.

Show the code one function for every change
  1. The markup. The app is one drawable element with a name, so it has one group to time.
  2. Every change goes through go(). The old picture has to be taken in a paint handler, before the transition starts.
  3. Draw from the old picture to the live app.
  4. The helper that keeps the canvas painting while a transition runs.

How it works

A view transition gives two things: timing (a set of CSS animations, one for each named element) and pictures (the old and new snapshots). Inside a canvas the pictures aren't available, because the canvas renders none of its contents and no call hands a snapshot to script. The timing is available. Experiments 1, 2 and 5 scope the transition to the canvas and read the group animations as clocks. Experiment 4 uses a document transition and reads the group's box. Experiment 3 leaves the moving to the browser and uses one canvas for each moving thing.

These run when this section is on screen, on the fixtures in the box below. Two of them start a transition on the whole document for under half a second. Nothing visible changes in it.

Findings

  • The canvas-scoped clock drives a WebGL shader. A WebGL canvas can be the scope of a transition like a 2D one. The shader gets one number for each tile, and CSS still sets the duration and easing. The page holds one WebGL context, through lib/element-gl.js.
  • Nesting works when the canvas has view-transition-scope: all all the time. Without it, a transition on an ancestor that is already running has taken the names inside the canvas, and a transition started on the canvas then is rejected with "Snapshot capture failed". Started in the other order, or in the same task, both run without it.
  • view-transition-class matches canvases in a scoped transition, so one rule times a list of canvases. Each canvas stays live in its new snapshot and can distort its own content while the browser moves it.
  • The group box of a canvas child can be drawn at, in a document transition. The canvas has to put the child's hit box back at its destination after each draw. If it does not, the group is retargeted to the place of the last draw every frame and stops moving.
  • One canvas can draw every change of an app. The old state is an ElementImage taken in a paint handler. It stays drawable after the DOM has changed, and can be drawn in pieces with the nine-argument drawElementImage().
  • The old state is a picture. In experiment 5 only the new state is live and takes input during the change. <live-transition> keeps both states live, at the cost of having both in the DOM.
